title: DNA triple-chain model failure
research_question: What precise molecular structure could explain nucleic acids using available chemical knowledge and X-ray information?
context: Pauling and Corey published a precise three-chain nucleic-acid structure in February 1953; the model was soon shown to be incorrect.
known_at_the_time: Nucleic acids contained phosphate, sugar and bases.
Available X-ray photographs constrained but did not uniquely determine the structure.
The proposed structure was precise enough to state atomic coordinates and compare with evidence.
unknown_at_the_time: The Watson-Crick double-helix solution and its later validation.
The full quality and implications of evidence that became decisive in the successful model.
trigger_or_anomaly: A race to formulate a precise nucleic-acid structure under incomplete evidence.
decision_action: Construct and publish a precise triple-chain structural model from general molecular-structure principles and the available nucleic-acid information, while acknowledging that detailed intensity calculations had not proved it correct.
observed_result: The proposed three-chain structure was incorrect and provides a counter-case for structural model building when decisive constraints or data checks are missing or violated.
alternative_interpretations: Failure should not be reduced to a single personality flaw; data access, competitive timing, model assumptions and chemical constraints all require separate historical review.
notes: Do not state exact causes such as specific missing measurements until contemporaneous primary records are inspected.
